title: Intel details 256-core Xeon 7 'Diamond Rapids', slips launch to 2027
subtitle: The 18A-P server flagship carries 1.28 GB of L3, DDR5-12800 MRDIMM support, and full AVX 10.2 — but drops hyperthreading and misses its original 2026 window.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Intel used its Hot Chips 2026 session at Stanford this week to detail the Xeon 7 'Diamond Rapids' platform. The flagship configuration carries up to 256 P-cores across 16 core-compute dies built on Intel's 18A-P process, four Intel 3-T base compute building blocks, and two Intel 3 fabric hub tiles, all connected with Foveros Direct and UCIe-S. Each base tile ships 320 MB of L3, totalling 1.28 GB across the package. Memory tops out at 16 channels of DDR5-8000, or 12,800 MT/s with MRDIMMs.

The disclosure matters because Diamond Rapids is Intel's answer to AMD's Turin-generation Epyc and, more critically, to the CPU workload that has re-emerged in the agentic-AI era. Intel added AMX FP8 support, the AVX 10.2 vector ISA, and the APX register-file extension — a stack aimed at inference orchestration, embedding, and mixed CPU-GPU pipelines. It also dropped hyperthreading entirely, betting that HPC and AI customers get more from wider vector units than from SMT.

The bad news alongside the deep dive was calendar slippage: Diamond Rapids will not ship in 2026 as originally planned, and Intel is now targeting a 2027 launch. That puts the flagship in the same window as AMD's Venice, Nvidia's Vera CPU, and the second generation of ARM-based hyperscaler silicon (Graviton 5, Cobalt 200, and Google's Axion successor). Intel is trying to reclaim the server socket that carried it for two decades, and it is doing so with less schedule cushion than any of those competitors.

For learners: the CPU has been treated as boring next to the GPU for the entire generative-AI cycle so far, but agentic workloads change the arithmetic. Every tool call, every retrieval, every long-context prep step runs on a CPU somewhere; the model itself is only one line on the flame graph. When Intel says AMX FP8 and AVX 10.2, they are pricing the assumption that AI inference is about to become a CPU story again. That thesis is worth understanding whether or not it's right.
